claim: The hair follicle (HF) growth cycle consists of three consecutive phases: anagen (active proliferation), catagen (apoptotic involution), and telogen (relative quiescence).
source: At the level of cellular activities, the hair growth cycle consists of three consecutive phases: anagen, phase of active proliferation; catagen, apoptotic involution phase; and telogen, relative quiescence phase (Al-Nuaimi et al., 2010; Paus and Foitzik, 2004; Schneider et al., 2009; Stenn and Paus, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing the three-phase hair cycle model.

claim: Cyclic regeneration of hair follicles is sustained by bulge stem cells located at the base of the permanent HF portion.
source: Cyclic regeneration is sustained by the bulge stem cells, located at the base of the permanent HF portion (Cotsarelis et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cotsarelis et al., 1990, which established the role of bulge stem cells.

claim: During anagen initiation, signals from the dermal papilla (DP) stimulate bulge stem cells and hair germ (HG) progenitors to proliferate.
source: During anagen initiation, signals from the niche, including the dermal papilla (DP), stimulate bulge stem cells and adjacent hair germ (HG) progenitors to proliferate (Enshell-Seijffers et al., 2010; Greco et al., 2009; Legrand et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies that established the role of DP signaling in anagen initiation.

claim: The bulge serves as a progenitor source, the matrix functions as a sink, and the ORS as a channel for progenitors transiting between them.
source: Conceptually, since the bulge produces downward migrating progeny (Hsu et al., 2011), it effectively serves as a progenitor source, while the matrix functions as a sink, and the ORS as a channel for progenitors transiting between them.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hsu et al., 2011 and represents a conceptual framework based on that work.

claim: BMP and WNT pathways constitute important components of the hair cycle clock.
source: Previous work on dorsal skin indicates that BMP and WNT pathways constitute important components of the hair cycle clock.
evidence: The claim is supported by prior work referenced in the manuscript and is further supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Defects in BMP or WNT pathways can dramatically change hair cycle progression.
source: Indeed, defects in either of these pathways can dramatically change hair cycle progression (Botchkarev et al., 2001a; Botchkarev and Sharov, 2004; Choi et al., 2013; Enshell-Seijffers et al., 2010; Kandyba and Kobielak, 2014; Kandyba et al., 2013; Kobielak et al., 2003, 2007; Sharov et al., 2005, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating effects of BMP and WNT pathway perturbations.

claim: Ligands and antagonists for BMP and WNT pathways mediate macro-environmental coordination between HFs.
source: and ligands and antagonists for both pathways mediate macro-environmental coordination between HFs (Chen et al., 2014; Plikus et al., 2011; Plikus and Chuong, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies that established the role of BMP and WNT ligands/antagonists in HF coordination.

claim: The combined signaling activities for multiple pathways partition the hair cycle in dorsal skin into four functional phases: propagating anagen (P), autonomous anagen (A), refractory telogen (R) and competent telogen (C).
source: Importantly, the combined signaling activities for the above pathways partition the hair cycle in the dorsal skin into four functional phases, each with its distinct activator/inhibitor profile: propagating anagen (P), autonomous anagen (A), refractory telogen (R) and competent telogen (C) (Hodgson et al., 2014; Plikus and Chuong, 2014; Plikus et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies that established the four-phase functional model.

claim: P-phase HFs can induce neighboring C-phase HFs to enter anagen via diffusible activators, leading to hair growth coupling.
source: Critical for this self-organization are the following HF-to-HF interactions: P-phase HFs can induce neighboring C-phase HFs to enter anagen via diffusible activators, leading to hair growth coupling, while A-phase anagen or R-phase telogen HFs cannot couple due to high levels of inhibitors (Murray et al., 2012; Plikus et al., 2011; Plikus and Chuong, 2014; Plikus et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four studies that established HF-to-HF interaction mechanisms.

claim: A-phase anagen or R-phase telogen HFs cannot couple due to high levels of inhibitors.
source: Critical for this self-organization are the following HF-to-HF interactions: P-phase HFs can induce neighboring C-phase HFs to enter anagen via diffusible activators, leading to hair growth coupling, while A-phase anagen or R-phase telogen HFs cannot couple due to high levels of inhibitors (Murray et al., 2012; Plikus et al., 2011; Plikus and Chuong, 2014; Plikus et al., 2008b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four studies that established HF-to-HF interaction mechanisms.

claim: Coupling inhibitors and activators with physical growth of HFs is sufficient to drive periodicity and excitability of hair regeneration.
source: Using multi-scale modeling, we show that coupling inhibitors and activators with physical growth of HFs is sufficient to drive periodicity and excitability of hair regeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1B.

claim: Mouse skin behaves as a heterogeneous regenerative field, composed of anatomical domains where HFs have distinct cycling dynamics.
source: Model simulations and experimental data reveal that mouse skin behaves as a heterogeneous regenerative field, composed of anatomical domains where HFs have distinct cycling dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by both model simulations and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2-4.

claim: Interactions between fast-cycling chin and ventral HFs and slow-cycling dorsal HFs produce bilaterally symmetric patterns.
source: Interactions between fast-cycling chin and ventral HFs and slow-cycling dorsal HFs produce bilaterally symmetric patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and modeling results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Ear skin behaves as a hyper-refractory domain with HFs in extended rest phase.
source: Ear skin behaves as a hyper-refractory domain with HFs in extended rest phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5 showing extended telogen in ear HFs.

claim: Hyper-refractivity of ear skin relates to high levels of BMP ligands and WNT antagonists, in part expressed by ear-specific cartilage and muscle.
source: Such hyper-refractivity relates to high levels of BMP ligands and WNT antagonists, in part expressed by ear-specific cartilage and muscle.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and reporter mouse studies presented in Figure 6.

claim: Hair growth stops at the boundaries with hyper-refractory ears and anatomically discontinuous eyelids, generating wave-breaking effects.
source: Hair growth stops at the boundaries with hyper-refractory ears and anatomically discontinuous eyelids, generating wave-breaking effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and modeling results presented in Figure 7.

claim: The model recognizes two phases determined by critical checkpoints: ~anagen and ~telogen.
source: Thus, our model recognizes two phases determined by these checkpoints: ~anagen, starting from the moment of activator amplification until anagen termination, and ~telogen, lasting until the next activator amplification event.
evidence: The claim describes the modeling framework and is supported by the model description and Figure 1.

claim: The cycle becomes autonomous and displays stable periodicity and excitability without a built-in 'clock'.
source: The cycle becomes autonomous – that is, it displays stable periodicity and excitability emerges naturally without a built-in 'clock' (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cycling is maintained within a range of parameter values, allowing testing for various intrinsic and extrinsic signaling scenarios.
source: Cycling is maintained within a range of parameter values, allowing testing for various intrinsic and extrinsic signaling scenarios (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The moving HF geometry in the model is critical, greatly contributing to the regulation of the cycle.
source: Simulations indicate that the moving HF geometry in the model is critical, greatly contributing to the regulation of the cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on model simulations and represents an inference from the modeling results.

claim: HF cycling occurs only within a certain range of signal strengths, the excitable regime.
source: Our model predicts that HF cycling occurs only within a certain range of signal strengths, that is the excitable regime (Figure 1C, white region).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Within the excitable regime, activator and inhibitor are predicted to inversely modulate duration of both ~telogen and ~anagen phases.
source: Within this regime, activator and inhibitor are predicted to inversely modulate duration of both ~telogen and ~anagen phases.
evidence: The claim is based on model predictions and is supported by Figure 1C.

claim: When inhibitor levels are very high, the HF is predicted to equilibrate in an extended telogen.
source: For example, when inhibitor levels are very high, the HF is predicted to equilibrate in an extended telogen (Appendix 2—figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Appendix 2—figure 5A.

claim: Extended anagen is predicted when inhibitor levels are very low.
source: while extended anagen is predicted for the opposite signaling condition (Appendix 2—figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by model predictions shown in Appendix 2—figure 5B.

claim: Model-predicted temporal dynamics for inhibitor and activator during ~anagen match the actual anagen expression dynamics for multiple BMP and WNT pathway members.
source: First, we found that model-predicted temporal dynamics for inhibitor and activator during ~anagen (Figure 1D and 1E) match the actual anagen expression dynamics for multiple BMP and WNT pathway members established on a highly temporally resolved whole-tissue dorsal skin microarray dataset (Lin et al., 2009) (Figure 1D–E''; Appendix 1-Identifying model predicted hair cycle activators and inhibitors).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model predictions with microarray data shown in Figure 1D-E''.

claim: Perturbing BMP and WNT in transgenic mice alters dorsal anagen phase duration and leads to hair length defects consistent with the model's predictions.
source: We also show that perturbing BMP (for details see Appendix 1-Validating model-predicted roles for BMP signaling in hair cycle control) and WNT in transgenic mice (for details see Appendix 1-Validating model-predicted roles for WNT signaling in hair cycle control) alters dorsal anagen phase duration and leads to hair length defects in a way that is consistent with the model's predictions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic mice described in the appendix.

claim: In a three-dimensional model where all HFs are assumed to be identical, full asynchrony evolves within just one cycle, and bilateral symmetry cannot be achieved.
source: We now show that in the three-dimensional model where all HFs are assumed to be identical, full asynchrony evolves within just one cycle, and bilateral symmetry cannot be achieved (Appendix 2-Dorsal and ventral HF patterns; Appendix 2—figures 11, 12; Appendix 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations shown in Appendix 2—figures 11, 12 and video 1.

claim: First anagen is inherently asynchronous as a result of spatially patterned HF development.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that first anagen is inherently asynchronous as a result of spatially patterned HF development.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the modeling results and is supported by subsequent experimental data.

claim: Spatial distribution of early anagen HFs in the dorsal skin of newborn mice reveals head-to-tail and subtle lateral-to-medial asynchronies.
source: Indeed, spatial distribution of early anagen HFs in the dorsal skin of newborn mice (Figure 2A–D) reveals head-to-tail and subtle lateral-to-medial asynchronies.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: Interactions between HFs across domain boundaries result in bilateral symmetry during the second cycle.
source: In simulations, interactions between HFs across domain boundaries result in bilateral symmetry during the second cycle (simulated time t68-78.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The model predicts that rapid hair growth pattern evolution requires interaction of two or more skin domains with distinct hair cycle parameters.
source: Taken together, the model predicts that rapid hair growth pattern evolution requires interaction of two or more skin domains with distinct hair cycle parameters.
evidence: The claim is a prediction from the model based on simulation results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Combined analysis from multiple Flash mice reveals prominent phase advancement in ventral over dorsal anagen during the second, third, and fourth hair cycles.
source: Combined analysis from multiple mice reveals prominent phase advancement in ventral over dorsal anagen, specifically during the second, third, and fourth hair cycles (Figure 3B, blue area).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioluminescence data from Flash mice shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spatial luminescence signal mapping reveals distinct ventral-to-dorsal anagen propagation with features of bilateral symmetry during second and third cycles.
source: Additionally, the spatial luminescence signal mapping reveals distinct ventral-to-dorsal anagen propagation with features of bilateral symmetry during second (Figure 3C; Appendix 1—figure 6) and third cycles (Figure 3C')
evidence: The claim is supported by bioluminescence mapping data shown in Figure 3C and 3C'.

claim: Ventrally, anagen phase is the shortest in the 'chin domain', ending around P10.
source: Ventrally, anagen phase is the shortest in the 'chin domain', ending around P10.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data described in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the ventral domain proper, anagen is longer, ending in the genital area around P14 and in the chest area around P17.
source: It is longer in the 'ventral domain' proper, ending in the genital area around P14 and in the chest area around P17 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Dorsally, anagen is the shortest in the 'cranial domain', ending around P14.
source: Dorsally, anagen is the shortest in the 'cranial domain', ending around P14.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data described in the text and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the dorsal domain proper, anagen ends as a head-to-tail wave between P15-P20.
source: In the 'dorsal domain' proper it ends as a head-to-tail wave between P15-P20 (Figure 3D; Appendix 1—figures 10, 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data shown in Figure 3D and Appendix 1—figures 10, 11.

claim: First ventral telogen is shorter than dorsal telogen.
source: First ventral telogen is shorter than dorsal telogen.
evidence: The claim is supported by the timing data presented in the text and figures.

claim: Second anagen initiates in the chin and ventral domains between P21-24 and then spreads toward ventral-dorsal boundaries in form of two bilaterally symmetric waves.
source: Second anagen initiates in the chin and ventral domains already between P21-24 and then spreads toward ventral-dorsal boundaries in form of two bilaterally symmetric waves (Figure 3E; Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data shown in Figure 3E and Appendix 1—figure 12.

claim: Second anagen ends faster in the ventral skin, maintaining ventral-dorsal asynchrony and bilateral symmetry.
source: Second anagen also ends faster in the ventral skin, maintaining ventral-dorsal asynchrony and bilateral symmetry (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Third anagen initiates the fastest in the chin domain, as early as P42.
source: Third anagen initiates the fastest in the chin domain, as early as P42 (Figures 3G and 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount skin analysis data shown in Figures 3G and 4H.

claim: Chin skin grafts showed faster cycling compared to dorsal skin grafts when transplanted onto the back of pigmented SCID mice.
source: When transplanted onto the back of pigmented SCID mice, chin skin grafts (n = 8) showed faster cycling compared to dorsal skin grafts (n = 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by skin grafting experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: While first post-transplantation anagen started with similar timing in both chin and dorsal grafts, consecutive anagen started significantly faster in chin grafts.
source: While first post-transplantation anagen started with similar timing in both chin and dorsal grafts, consecutive anagen started significantly faster in chin grafts (Figure 3H and I; Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by skin grafting experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I and Appendix 1—figure 13.

claim: Faster hair cycle dynamics in chin and ventral domains is a property that is partially maintained upon skin grafting.
source: Underlying this behavior are faster hair growth cycle dynamics in chin and ventral HFs, a property that is partially maintained upon skin grafting.
evidence: The claim is supported by the skin grafting experimental data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed non-overlapping transcriptomic trajectories of the hair cycle between chin, ventral, and dorsal domains.
source: Analysis revealed non-overlapping transcriptomic trajectories of the hair cycle between the three domains (Figure 4A–B'')
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A-B''.

claim: Chin, ventral, and dorsal domains show domain-specific expression patterns for multiple putative activator and inhibitor genes at all hair cycle time points.
source: and domain-specific expression patterns for multiple putative activator and inhibitor genes at all hair cycle time points (Appendix 1—figures 14–19; Dataset 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Appendix 1—figures 14–19 and Dataset 2.

claim: Chin and ventral domains show enrichment for gene ontologies related to macrophage function and lipid storage during early telogen.
source: Differential gene expression analysis (Figure 4C–D) revealed enrichment in chin and ventral domains for gene ontologies related to macrophage function and lipid storage
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Chin domain shows enrichment for muscle-related genes during early telogen.
source: and enrichment in chin domain for muscle-related genes (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Chin skin shows more contractile cells around HFs compared to dorsal skin.
source: Consistently, chin skin shows more contractile cells around HFs
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Appendix 1—figures 20, 21.

claim: Chin and ventral skin have thicker dermal adipose tissue compared to dorsal skin.
source: and chin and ventral skin have thicker dermal adipose tissue and substantially more CD11b+;F4/80+ macrophages as compared to dorsal skin (Appendix 1—figures 20, 21).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Appendix 1—figures 20, 21.

claim: Chin and ventral skin have substantially more CD11b+;F4/80+ macrophages compared to dorsal skin.
source: and chin and ventral skin have thicker dermal adipose tissue and substantially more CD11b+;F4/80+ macrophages as compared to dorsal skin (Appendix 1—figures 20, 21).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological and FACS data shown in Appendix 1—figures 20, 21.

claim: Dorsal early telogen skin shows gene expression changes consistent with higher refractivity, including enrichment for several BMP ligands and depletion for BMP antagonists and WNT ligands.
source: Furthermore, dorsal early telogen skin shows gene expression changes consistent with higher refractivity – it is enriched for several BMP ligands, and depleted for BMP antagonists and WNT ligands (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In Axin2-lacZ WNT reporter mice, many more HFs with WNT-active DPs are seen in chin and ventral as compared to dorsal skin at P36.
source: Consistently, in Axin2-lacZ WNT reporter mice, many more HFs with WNT-active DPs are seen in chin and ventral as compared to dorsal skin at P36 (Figure 4G; Appendix 1—figure 22A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 4G and Appendix 1—figure 22A.

claim: WNT activity increases in dorsal skin to the levels of ventral skin by P42.
source: WNT activity increases in dorsal skin to the levels of ventral skin only by P42 (Figure 4H; Appendix 1—figure 22B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 4H and Appendix 1—figure 22B.

claim: In P42 BRE-gal BMP reporter mice, many more HFs with BMP-active bulges are seen in dorsal as compared to chin and ventral skin.
source: Furthermore, in P42 BRE-gal BMP reporter mice, many more HFs with BMP-active bulges are seen in dorsal as compared to chin and ventral skin (Figure 4I; Appendix 1—figure 22C).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 4I and Appendix 1—figure 22C.

claim: In Krt14-Wnt7a mice, spontaneous anagen initiation sites in dorsal skin overrun ventral-to-dorsal wave dominance.
source: In Krt14-Wnt7a mice, spontaneous anagen initiation sites in dorsal skin overrun ventral-to-dorsal wave dominance (Figure 4J; Appendix 1—figure 23).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic mouse data shown in Figure 4J and Appendix 1—figure 23.

claim: In Krt14-Bmp4 mice, ventral-dorsal hair growth waves stall and asymmetric anagen patches form instead.
source: In contrast, in Krt14-Bmp4 mice, ventral-dorsal hair growth waves stall and asymmetric anagen patches form instead (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic mouse data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Lower refractivity and the underlying differences in BMP and WNT activities form the bases for ventral-dorsal hair growth dominance.
source: Together, this data confirms that lower refractivity and the underlying differences in BMP and WNT activities form the bases for ventral-dorsal hair growth dominance.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: In the ear skin, HF morphogenesis begins between days P2-P4.
source: In the ear skin, HF morphogenesis begins between days P2-P4
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ear HFs remain in anagen until about P15.
source: and HFs remain in anagen until about P15 (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: After first anagen, ear HFs remain in an extended telogen for at least three months.
source: After first anagen, and for at least three months, they remain in an extended telogen, while at the same time dorsal HFs have already reached their third cycle (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole mount ear skin analysis data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Anagen waves spreading from cranial skin could not propagate into ear skin.
source: Moreover, anagen waves spreading from cranial skin could not propagate into ear skin (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Dorsal telogen HFs readily respond to cyclosporin A treatment.
source: We show that while dorsal telogen HFs readily respond to cyclosporin A (Appendix 1—figure 27B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 27B.

claim: Ear HFs remain quiescent even 3 weeks after cyclosporin A treatment.
source: ear HFs remain quiescent even 3 weeks after treatment (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Ear HFs can be induced to enter anagen in response to SAG, but this response occurs late, after 3 weeks, and remains restricted to the medial side of the ear.
source: Anagen can be induced in response to SAG; however, this response occurs late, after 3 weeks, and remains restricted to the medial side of the ear (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dorsal skin shows rapid SAG-induced anagen.
source: This is contrasted by rapid SAG-induced anagen in dorsal skin (Appendix 1—figure 27A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 27A.

claim: Plucking induces anagen along the medial side of the ear, but there is no anagen wave spreading into the unplucked region.
source: Plucking induces anagen along the medial side of the ear; however, there is no anagen wave spreading into the unplucked region, a feature common in dorsal skin (Chen et al., 2015) (Figure 5D; Appendix 1—figures 25A-B, 26).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Appendix 1—figures 25A-B, 26.

claim: Whole ear plucking experiments reveal very sparse anagen activation along the lateral side.
source: Furthermore, whole ear plucking experiments reveal very sparse anagen activation along the lateral side (Appendix 1—figure 25C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Appendix 1—figure 25C.

claim: Adult ear HFs equilibrate in a hyper-refractory telogen state physiologically, yet remain capable of regenerative cycling in response to selective external stimuli.
source: These data demonstrate that physiologically, adult ear HFs equilibrate in a hyper-refractory telogen state, yet in principle remain capable of regenerative cycling in response to selective external stimuli.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Transcriptomes of first telogen ear skin, first telogen dorsal skin and ear cartilage/muscle complex are distinct.
source: We show that, transcriptionally, these three tissue types are distinct (Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and PCA analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ear skin, dorsal skin, and cartilage/muscle complex contain 1334 differentially expressed genes.
source: containing large number of differentially expressed genes (Figure 6B; Dataset 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6B and Dataset 3.

claim: Ear skin, dorsal skin, and cartilage/muscle complex show enrichment for distinct gene ontologies.
source: enriched for distinct gene ontologies (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Compared to dorsal skin, ear skin is enriched for transcripts for several WNT antagonists, including Dkkl1, Dkk2 and Sfrp2.
source: Compared to dorsal skin, ear skin is enriched for transcripts for several WNT antagonists, including Dkkl1, Dkk2 and Sfrp2
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Ear skin is enriched for collagen Col17a1, implicated in HF stem cell maintenance.
source: as well as collagen Col17a1, implicated in HF stem cell maintenance (Matsumura et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and a citation to Matsumura et al., 2016.

claim: Cartilage/muscle complex is prominently enriched for Bmp5.
source: Cartilage/muscle complex is prominently enriched for Bmp5
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cartilage/muscle complex is enriched for multiple WNT antagonists, including Frzb, Sfrp2, Sfrp5 and Wif1.
source: and multiple WNT antagonists, including Frzb, Sfrp2, Sfrp5 and Wif1.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cartilage/muscle complex showed upregulated expression of Fgf18, a known hair cycle inhibitor.
source: Additionally, it showed upregulated expression of other known hair cycle inhibitors Fgf18 (Kimura-Ueki et al., 2012; Leishman et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to studies establishing Fgf18 as a hair cycle inhibitor.

claim: Cartilage/muscle complex showed upregulated expression of Ctgf, a known hair cycle inhibitor.
source: and Ctgf (Liu and Leask, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and a citation to Liu and Leask, 2013.

claim: BRE-gal reporter reveals high BMP activity in telogen ear HFs and in the adjacent cartilage/muscle complex.
source: Using BRE-gal reporter mice, we show high levels of BMP activity in telogen ear HFs (in the bulge), as well as in the cartilage and muscle (Figure 6F and F').
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 6F and F'.

claim: Axin2-lacZ reporter reveals isolated sites of WNT activity in ear skin dermis, and a lack of activity in telogen HFs as well as in the cartilage and muscle.
source: Using Axin2-lacZ reporter mice, we show isolated sites of WNT activity in ear skin dermis, and a lack of activity in telogen HFs as well as in the cartilage and muscle (Figure 6G and G').
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter mouse data shown in Figure 6G and G'.

claim: Overexpression of the BMP antagonist Noggin in Krt14-Noggin mice partially rescued the hyper-refractory state, with substantially more spontaneous anagen HFs found compared to wild-type control.
source: Overexpression of the BMP antagonist Noggin in Krt14-Noggin mice partially rescued the hyper-refractory state – substantially more spontaneous anagen HFs can be found in Krt14-Noggin ears as compared to wild-type control (Figure 6H and H'; Appendix 1—figure 28B, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic mouse data shown in Figure 6H and H' and Appendix 1—figure 28B, D.

claim: Wnt7a overexpression in Krt14-Wnt7a mice reactivated anagen in ear skin, albeit to a lesser extent compared to Noggin overexpression.
source: Wnt7a overexpression in Krt14-Wnt7a mice also reactivated anagen in ear skin, albeit to a lesser extent compared to Noggin overexpression (Figure 6H''; Appendix 1—figure 28C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic mouse data shown in Figure 6H'' and Appendix 1—figure 28C, D.

claim: Hyper-refractivity of ear HFs depends on higher levels of BMP ligands and WNT antagonists, in part produced by the cartilage/muscle complex.
source: Together, these results support that hyper-refractivity of ear HFs depends on higher levels of BMP ligands and WNT antagonists, in part produced by the cartilage/muscle complex (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The model predicts that hair growth waves can form distorted patterns around non-propagating skin regions, such as hyper-refractory hair-bearing skin or hairless skin.
source: Lastly, our model predicts that hair growth waves can form distorted patterns around non-propagating skin regions, such as hyper-refractory hair-bearing skin or hairless skin (Figure 7A and B; Appendix 2-Hyper-refractory domain and Wave breaker; Appendix 2—figure 17; Appendix 2—video 5).
evidence: The claim is a prediction from the model shown in Figure 7A and B and Appendix 2—figure 17.

claim: Hair growth waves prominently break around the eyelids and ears, with anagen waves propagating faster through the hair-bearing skin around these structures and then distorting into the spaces in front of them.
source: Indeed, we observe that hair growth waves prominently break around the eyelids and ears – anagen waves propagate faster through the hair-bearing skin around the eyelids and ears, and then distort into the spaces in front of these anatomical structures (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7C and E.

claim: Similar wave distortion patterns are observed for the ventral-to-dorsal hair growth wave around the limbs.
source: Similar patterns are also observed for the ventral-to-dorsal hair growth wave around the limbs (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Distortions of hair growth waves around anatomical structures with temporary or permanent non-propagating properties contribute to rapid body-wide hair growth pattern evolution.
source: We conclude that distortions of hair growth waves around anatomical structures with temporary or permanent non-propagating properties contribute to rapid body-wide hair growth pattern evolution.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and modeling data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The multiscale model allows incorporation of differential HF growth in space, a feature required for simulating heterogeneous skin properties.
source: Importantly, however, only our model allows incorporation of differential HF growth in space, a feature required for simulating heterogeneous skin properties such as interactions between skin domains with different hair cycle frequencies or the hair wave distortion effect.
evidence: The claim describes a key feature of the model and is supported by the modeling results throughout the manuscript.

claim: First anagen entry by ventral HFs is delayed by approximately 3 days compared to dorsal HFs and proceeds as a concentric lateral-to-midline wave.
source: In fact, we show that the first cycle is already distinctly patterned: at birth, anagen HFs in dorsal skin have head-to-tail and lateral-to-medial asynchronies, while first anagen entry by ventral HFs is delayed by approximately 3 days and proceeds as a concentric lateral-to-midline wave.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: First anagen entry by ear HFs is delayed by 6 days compared to dorsal HFs.
source: Similarly delayed by 6 days are ear HFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HF morphogenesis is spatially asynchronous.
source: Our findings of spatial asynchrony of the first anagen indicate spatial asynchrony of HF morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observed spatial asynchrony of first anagen.

claim: During early postnatal cycles, chin and ventral domains become the dominant sources of skin-wide anagen waves.
source: Specifically, we show that during early postnatal cycles, chin and ventral domains become the dominant sources of skin-wide anagen waves.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Dominant behavior of chin and ventral domains is accompanied by distinct activity dynamics for WNT and BMP, putative hair cycle activators and inhibitors, respectively.
source: Such dominant behavior of chin and ventral domains is accompanied by distinct activity dynamics for WNT and BMP, putative hair cycle activators and inhibitors, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq and reporter mouse data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transgenic mouse studies confirm the functional importance of differential WNT and BMP activities in setting distinct hair growth pace across discrete anatomical skin regions.
source: Transgenic mouse studies further confirm the functional importance of differential WNT and BMP activities in setting distinct hair growth pace across discrete anatomical skin regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by transgenic mouse data shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: Novel behaviors can be produced by the cooption of signals from new tissue modules, rather than by the modification of preexisting ones.
source: Thus, novel behaviors can be produced by the cooption of signals from new tissue modules, rather than by the modification of preexisting ones.
evidence: The claim is a general principle inferred from the finding that ear cartilage/muscle complex produces signals affecting ear HF behavior.

claim: Non-HF cell types can have modulatory effects on the dorsal skin hair cycle, including adipose progenitors, mature adipocytes, and resident macrophages.
source: This finding parallels the modulatory effects of non-HF cell types on the dorsal skin hair cycle, including adipose progenitors (Festa et al., 2011; Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016), mature adipocytes (Plikus et al., 2008b), and resident macrophages (Castellana et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies establishing these modulatory effects.

claim: The skin as a whole functions as a complex regenerative landscape with regions of fast, slow, and very slow hair renewal.
source: Taken together, our study reveals that the skin as a whole functions as a complex regenerative landscape with regions of fast, slow, and very slow hair renewal (Appendix 1—figure 29).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental and modeling data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Variable hair density in the fur coat likely serves an adaptive role, such as in thermoregulation.
source: We show that this behavior produces a fur coat with variable hair density, which likely serves an adaptive role, such as in thermoregulation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential adaptive function for the observed hair density variation.

claim: The WNT/BMP activator/inhibitor signaling pair modulates hair regeneration in all skin regions studied.
source: Mechanistically, we show that the WNT/BMP activator/inhibitor signaling pair modulates hair regeneration in all skin regions studied.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple skin regions shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: The WNT/BMP 'molecular language' for hair growth is general, rather than a special case for a specific body site.
source: This suggests that the WNT/BMP 'molecular language' for hair growth is general, rather than a special case for a specific body site.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that WNT/BMP signaling modulates hair regeneration across all studied skin regions.

claim: The generality of the WNT/BMP molecular language allows for hair-to-hair communications to arise across anatomic domain boundaries.
source: Its generality allows for hair-to-hair communications to arise across anatomic domain boundaries, which, in turn, enables novel hair growth dynamics not obvious from prior work – fast cycling skin regions (such as chin skin) function as a kind of hair growth pacemaker.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental and modeling data.

claim: Fast cycling skin regions (such as chin skin) function as a kind of hair growth pacemaker.
source: Its generality allows for hair-to-hair communications to arise across anatomic domain boundaries, which, in turn, enables novel hair growth dynamics not obvious from prior work – fast cycling skin regions (such as chin skin) function as a kind of hair growth pacemaker.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing chin and ventral domains as dominant sources of anagen waves.

claim: The signaling macro-environment function can include any closely-positioned anatomic structures with signaling properties, such as cartilage.
source: Furthermore, our findings on ear hair cycle expand the repertoire of tissues with signaling macro-environment function to include any closely-positioned anatomic structures with signaling properties, such as cartilage.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the finding that ear cartilage/muscle complex affects ear HF behavior.

claim: Some of the newly found hair regeneration features can have analogs in other organs.
source: We posit that some of the newly found hair regeneration features can have analogs in other organs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential parallels in other organs.

claim: Dominant anatomically defined pacemakers are common in electrically coupled muscle-based tissues, including heart and stomach, where they generate directional contractile rhythmicity.
source: For instance, dominant anatomically defined pacemakers are common in the electrically coupled muscle-based tissues, including heart and stomach, where they generate directional contractile rhythmicity.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about pacemakers in muscle-based tissues.

claim: Other actively regenerating organs, such as the intestines and bone marrow, can likely contain anatomic regions of faster and slower regeneration that can be coupled to work in coordination.
source: Other actively regenerating organs, such as the intestines and bone marrow, can likely contain anatomic regions of faster and slower regeneration and, conceivably, they can be coupled to work in coordination.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential parallels in other regenerating organs.

claim: Knowledge learned from the skin system can guide the search for regenerative landscapes in other organs.
source: Knowledge learned from the skin system in the current study can guide the search for regenerative landscapes in these and other organs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential applications of the findings to other organs.

claim: Coordination principles observed in the skin may be universal and likely operate in other organs despite prominent anatomical differences.
source: Because coordination principles observed in the skin may be universal, the likelihood of them operating in other organs is substantial despite prominent anatomical differences.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting potential universality of the observed coordination principles.

claim: The modeling framework is based on a hybrid approach, with individual HFs modeled as an expanding or contracting one-dimensional line and with diffusive molecules described in reaction-diffusion equations.
source: The modeling framework is based on a hybrid approach, with individual HFs modeled as an expanding or contracting one-dimensional line and with the diffusive molecules described in reaction-diffusion equations (Appendix 2, Equations 1–4).
evidence: The claim describes the computational modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Guard, awl, auchene and zigzag club hair types were measured for hair length analysis.
source: Guard, awl, auchene and zigzag club hair types were photographed, traced and calibrated using Adobe Illustrator software.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental methods used for hair length measurements.

claim: RNA samples with RIN >8.0 were considered for cDNA library preparation.
source: RNA samples with RIN >8.0 were considered for cDNA library preparation.
evidence: The claim describes the quality control criteria for RNA-seq sample preparation.
